note: Hand-verified ministerial controversies, May 2022 onward. Each entry: what happened (as reported), the minister's/government's response, and the outcome, with at least two reputable sources. Categories are descriptive labels, not findings by this site.

items.portfolio: Prime Minister
items.title: PM's 'melons' podcast remark about Japanese PM Takaichi's gift draws apology demands
items.summary: On comedian Nikki Osborne's Bush Deep podcast (released early July 2026), Albanese recalled being gifted two crown melons by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi during her May 2026 visit, describing the gift as 'pretty strange' but 'quite good'. Osborne joked 'She brought two. She just came in looking like Pamela Anderson'; Albanese replied 'She brought two, and they're beautiful' while gesturing with his hands, which critics read as mimicking a woman's chest. An AAP FactCheck (13 July) found the Pamela Anderson comparison was made by Osborne, not the PM. The issue escalated on 10 August when former Japanese ambassador Shingo Yamagami criticised the remarks in The Australian and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor demanded a personal apology to Takaichi. On 12 August an internal Japanese government memo, which said Japan saw no 'ill intention' and would not raise the matter, was leaked to Australian media; Liberal senator James Paterson referred the leak to the AFP.
items.response: The PM's office said the assertion that he mimicked Takaichi's body 'is incorrect'. In Parliament Albanese said 'I reject the assertion in the question' and that 'Prime Minister Takaichi is a friend of Australia and a friend of mine'. Japan's ambassador Kazuhiro Suzuki said Japan had been 'informed by the Australian side that Prime Minister Albanese did not make the comments in the way that has been reported'.
items.outcome: No apology to Takaichi; no formal finding. Japan did not formally raise the matter. AFP acknowledged a referral over the memo leak (not over the PM's conduct). Albanese separately conceded appearing on the podcast was 'an error'.

items.portfolio: Prime Minister
items.title: PM apologises 'unequivocally' for 'shag, marry, date' answer about Kylie Minogue
items.summary: In an episode of Nikki Osborne's Bush Deep podcast released on Friday 3 July 2026, Albanese was asked to play 'shag, marry, date' with Kylie Minogue, Nicole Kidman and Rhonda Burchmore. He initially declined, citing his recent marriage, but when pressed on a hypothetical said 'Oh, Kylie clearly' and, asked whether he would marry, shag and date her, replied 'All of the above'. He also made remarks about his own sex life. Community Strong MP Zali Steggall called his participation 'entirely inappropriate'; Liberal senator Sarah Henderson called it 'crude locker room talk'.
items.response: On Monday 6 July Albanese issued a statement: 'I apologise unequivocally for the comments.' He later said appearing on the podcast was 'an error'. Acting PM Richard Marles and Tanya Plibersek defended his record on gender equality.
items.outcome: Public apology; no formal finding. Minogue did not comment publicly.

items.portfolio: Minister for Climate Change and Energy
items.title: Bowen's overseas travel bill and COP31 department travel questioned by Opposition
items.summary: Documents obtained by The Australian (reported by AAP, 26 May 2026) showed climate department staff were authorised to spend $485,602 on travel to Turkey, Fiji, Germany and Korea in January–February 2026 in preparation for Australia's COP31 role, with the overall COP31 role budgeted at more than $150 million. On 6 August 2026 News Corp outlets reported IPEA data showing Bowen and accompanying staff spent $345,000 over 46 days of international travel in 2025–26, including a $118,030 nine-day US visit, $79,233 to Brazil and Chile, $45,052 to Denmark, Finland and Singapore and $41,443 to Germany and Singapore. Opposition energy spokesman Dan Tehan said Bowen should explain how the spending had 'led to cheaper power bills'.
items.response: Bowen called Tehan 'the biggest hypocrite in the federal parliament', citing Tehan's own ministerial travel. Bowen's spokesperson said the minister 'regularly engages with counterparts ... via videoconference' and that 'international travel is used only when other communication means are deemed ineffective'.
items.outcome: No formal finding; travel reported through IPEA as within entitlements.

items.portfolio: Minister for Veterans' Affairs and Defence Personnel
items.title: Keogh reverses Budget decision to end $9m Invictus Australia funding after outcry
items.summary: The 12 May 2026 Budget did not renew a $9 million, three-year funding commitment (about $3 million a year since 2022–23) to Invictus Australia, which runs sport-based recovery programs for veterans. Invictus Australia CEO Michael Hartung called it 'a devastating blow' and said Australia might not field a team for the 2027 Birmingham Games; athlete Vanessa Broughill told the ABC the cut 'can be life-threatening'.
items.response: Keogh initially said the grant program had concluded and the new Veteran and Family Wellbeing Agency would 'provide future opportunities to work with the sector to develop a competitive program'. On 28 May 2026 he announced on A Current Affair that funding would continue for a further three years.
items.outcome: Decision reversed on 28 May 2026; funding reinstated for three years. The reversal was later cited by the Opposition as one of several Keogh 'backflips'.

items.portfolio: Minister for Veterans' Affairs and Defence Personnel
items.title: Keogh's $5,000 veterans' allied-health cap scrapped after four months of backlash
items.summary: The May 2026 Budget (12 May) introduced a $5,000 annual threshold on DVA-funded allied health services (e.g. physiotherapy, dentistry) for veterans from 1 July 2027, replacing the existing 12-visit GP re-referral rule; the measure was linked to savings reported at roughly $700–779 million over four years. RSL Australia and ten national ex-service organisations issued a joint open letter opposing it, and the Senate passed an urgency motion (8 September) and reversal amendments (10 September). In Parliament on 18–20 August 2026, Keogh apologised for initially declining to meet a veterans' delegation (the Coalition of Veterans' Voices), whose members accused him of refusing to shake hands and rolling his eyes at the eventual meeting; the Coalition attempted to censure him.
items.response: On 17 September 2026 Keogh said: 'We have been consulting on this measure, and we have heard from veterans there are concerns about this approach,' and confirmed the threshold was 'off the table'. He had earlier told Parliament he 'got it wrong' by declining the meeting.
items.outcome: Policy withdrawn on 17 September 2026 before taking effect. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it had 'taken too long' and called for Keogh to resign; no resignation. A related $9 million Invictus Australia funding cut in the same Budget was also reversed (see separate entry).

items.portfolio: Prime Minister
items.title: PM describes Grace Tame as 'difficult' in word-association game, issues qualified apology
items.summary: At the Future Victoria conference in Melbourne on Wednesday 25 February 2026, Albanese took part in a rapid-fire one-word association segment and answered 'difficult' when given the name of Grace Tame, the 2021 Australian of the Year and child sexual abuse survivor advocate. Greens senators Larissa Waters and Sarah Hanson-Young criticised the label. Tame wrote on Instagram that the term is 'a misogynist's code for a woman who won't comply' and, after his apology, called it 'a patronising cop out from a total coward'.
items.response: Albanese said on 26 February: 'If there was any misinterpretation, then I certainly apologise. She has had a difficult life and that was what I was referring to.' He also criticised Tame's chanting of 'globalise the intifada' at a rally.
items.outcome: Qualified apology; no formal finding.

items.portfolio: Attorney-General (Communications Minister at time of travel)
items.title: Rowland repays about $10,000 after IPEA finds Perth family trip partly outside guidelines
items.summary: The Australian Financial Review reported in December 2025 that Rowland had billed taxpayers more than $21,000 for a week-long trip to Perth in July 2023, including $16,050 in family-reunion flights; the trip began with around 10 official engagements before a family holiday. Rowland referred the claims to the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority, which advised on 12 December 2025 that 'a portion of the family reunion travel expenses were outside the guidelines'.
items.response: Rowland's office said she 'formally accepted that advice' and 'commenced steps to make a repayment'. She later expressed regret, saying it 'shouldn't have happened'.
items.outcome: IPEA finding of partial non-compliance; Rowland repaid $7,932 in airfares plus a 25% penalty of $1,983 (about $10,000), confirmed 4 March 2026.

items.portfolio: Minister for Trade and Tourism; Special Minister of State
items.title: Farrell named highest user of family travel entitlements at $48,178 in 2024–25
items.summary: An ABC analysis of IPEA data (10 December 2025) found Farrell, the minister responsible for setting parliamentary expense rules, was the largest user of family-reunion travel in 2024–25 at $48,178 ($29,966 Canberra flights, $14,953 other domestic flights, $3,258 car costs); AAP reported his family travel exceeded $90,000 since 2022. Claims included family travel to Uluru, to Sydney coinciding with an opera performance, to Melbourne during a theatre premiere, and $5,760 for attending the 2023 and 2024 AFL grand finals with a family member. No breach of IPEA rules was alleged.
items.response: Farrell defended the travel as within the rules and tied to his tourism and trade duties, including presenting graduation certificates to Indigenous hospitality workers at Uluru.
items.outcome: No formal finding. The Remuneration Tribunal tightened family travel rules in January 2026 (economy-class only for spouses; non-Canberra family trips limited).

items.portfolio: Minister for Communications and Minister for Sport
items.title: Wells' taxpayer-funded travel to sporting events audited; four breaches, $10,116 repaid
items.summary: In December 2025 the ABC, AFR and The Nightly reported Wells had charged taxpayers for family travel coinciding with sponsored tickets to AFL grand finals (2022–2025), Boxing Day Tests, the Australian Open and a Thredbo ski trip; Comcar waits of several hours at events; a $3,681 Adelaide trip that included a friend's birthday; three Paris trips totalling about $116,000 for the Rugby World Cup, Olympics and Paralympics; and, per The Nightly, at least $62,000 for 60-plus sporting events since 2022. On 9 December she self-referred 3.5 years of claims to IPEA. IPEA's 268-page audit of about 250 claims (8 May 2026) found four breaches: $1,208.98 for her husband's flights in February 2022, $5,513.37 for family flights and car hire three days before her ministerial swearing-in in May 2025, $726.29 for her husband's flight home the day after the 2025 AFL Grand Final, and $644.25 in car hire in regional NSW in October 2025. The Thredbo trip was found compliant.
items.response: In December Wells said: 'I absolutely accept those figures prompt a gut reaction in people' but that she had 'upheld' the rules. After the audit she said: 'I chose what I thought was the more sensible, cheaper option, but those choices were not allowed according to the rules, which I accept and respect ... I am sorry for making these honest mistakes.'
items.outcome: IPEA found four breaches; Wells repaid $10,116 ($8,093 plus a 25% penalty of $2,023). IPEA introduced new advance flagging of high-cost bookings. Wells remained in the ministry.

items.portfolio: Minister for Communications and Minister for Sport
items.title: Wells' $94,828 business-class flights to New York for UN social-media-ban speech
items.summary: Senate estimates figures reported in early December 2025 showed $94,828 was spent on business-class flights for Wells and two staff to attend the UN General Assembly in September 2025 to promote Australia's under-16 social media ban; the total trip cost was about $118,000. Wells delayed her departure two days after the Optus Triple Zero outage, and flights were rebooked at short notice on Air New Zealand. FOI documents released in February 2026 showed the rebooking added about $7,000 and that neither IPEA nor the travel agent flagged the fares. The Prime Minister confirmed his office approved the changed travel.
items.response: Wells said: 'I had to be in two places at once. It was a really tricky situation' and that 'people can have an opinion about whether it was worth the money'. Albanese said: 'We make decisions as a government. We spoke in the morning, and the minister travelled.'
items.outcome: IPEA's May 2026 audit found the New York trip compliant, noting Wells had 'very limited' alternative flight options; no repayment required for this trip.

items.portfolio: Prime Minister (allegations relate to period as Transport Minister/shadow minister)
items.title: Book alleges PM sought Qantas upgrades from Alan Joyce; PM denies ever calling him
items.summary: Joe Aston's book The Chairman's Lounge (October 2024) alleged Albanese received at least 22 free Qantas upgrades over more than a decade, liaised directly with then-CEO Alan Joyce about his personal travel, and in 2022 asked Joyce to give his son Nathan Chairman's Lounge membership. Opposition Leader Peter Dutton said Albanese should refer himself to the National Anti-Corruption Commission, and Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie sought disclosure of the number and value of upgrades. Independent senator David Pocock criticised the PM for taking several days to clarify.
items.response: Albanese said: 'From time to time, members of parliament receive upgrades. What's important is that they are declared. All of mine have been declared.' On 30 October his office said: 'The prime minister did not ever call Alan Joyce seeking an upgrade.' He described the claims as rumours 'to sell a book'.
items.outcome: No NACC referral or formal finding; upgrades were declared on the register of interests. Senate crossbench considered but did not establish a specific inquiry.

items.portfolio: Prime Minister
items.title: PM buys $4.3 million Copacabana clifftop home during housing affordability debate
items.summary: On 15 October 2024 it was reported that Albanese was buying a four-bedroom clifftop house at Copacabana on the NSW Central Coast for $4.3 million, near his fiancée Jodie Haydon's family, partly funded by selling an inner-west investment property. Opposition Leader Peter Dutton said the purchase was 'a matter for the prime minister' but that he was worried about 'people who can't afford their mortgages'; Greens housing spokesman Max Chandler-Mather criticised 'property investor politicians'. A senior Labor source was quoted comparing it to Scott Morrison's Hawaii holiday.
items.response: Albanese said: 'When your relationship changes, your life changes' and 'As a prime minister, I earn a good income. I understand that I've been fortunate,' adding 'I know what it is like to struggle. My mum lived in the one public housing that she was born in for all of her 65 years.'
items.outcome: No formal finding; a matter of political judgement rather than rules.

items.portfolio: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence
items.title: Marles' chief of staff says she was sidelined after raising bullying complaint
items.summary: On 10 October 2024 Jo Tarnawsky, Marles' chief of staff, publicly alleged that after she raised concerns about bullying by a senior colleague during a flight home from Ukraine in April 2024, Marles told her the situation was not 'fixable', directed her to take leave and seek other employment, and she was subsequently locked out of the office for more than 200 days without an investigation. On 25 November 2024 she filed Federal Court proceedings for adverse action against the Commonwealth, Marles and the Prime Minister's chief of staff. She did not allege Marles himself bullied her.
items.response: Asked in Parliament whether he had complied with the Ministerial Code of Conduct, Marles said: 'The short answer to the question is I am satisfied.' His spokesperson said 'a number of her assertions and recollections are contested' and that she had 'been treated with respect and courtesy'.
items.outcome: Federal Court proceedings commenced November 2024; no adverse finding against Marles reported.

items.portfolio: Minister for the NDIS and Minister for Government Services
items.title: Services Australia's $620,000 two-year speechwriter contract for Shorten questioned
items.summary: Senate estimates in June 2024 revealed Services Australia had awarded a contract worth about $620,499 over two years (around $300,000 a year) to speechwriter Julianne Stewart to write for the agency and for Shorten, with $447,516 paid after 20 months. The agency said it faced 'market failure' when recruiting in July 2022 and could not say who proposed the contract. Coalition figures Paul Fletcher and James Stevens called it 'bizarre' and 'ridiculous', contrasting it with Shorten's push to reduce NDIS spending.
items.response: Shorten said he had 'no idea what the payment was', that 'I'm not responsible for negotiating a contract' and that the speechwriter 'does a very good job' including training and mentoring staff.
items.outcome: No formal finding; the contract was a departmental procurement.

items.portfolio: Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs
items.title: Giles' Direction 99 blamed for tribunal reinstating visas of serious offenders
items.summary: Ministerial Direction 99, issued by Giles in early 2023 after commitments to New Zealand, required decision-makers to weigh a non-citizen's ties to Australia when considering visa cancellations. In May 2024 it emerged the Administrative Appeals Tribunal had cited the direction when reinstating visas of people convicted of serious offences, including a man later charged with murder in Brisbane. The Coalition called for Giles' resignation over several weeks of Question Time.
items.response: Giles acknowledged the direction 'has not produced, in the AAT decisions, the outcomes that we expected' but refused to resign; the government re-cancelled a number of visas and announced a replacement direction.
items.outcome: Direction 99 replaced by Direction 110 on 7 June 2024, prioritising community safety. Giles was moved from the immigration portfolio in the July 2024 reshuffle.

items.portfolio: Minister for Home Affairs (with Immigration Minister Andrew Giles)
items.title: NZYQ detainee releases: O'Neil corrects 'legal advice' remark amid 'botched' claims
items.summary: After the High Court's 8 November 2023 NZYQ ruling that indefinite immigration detention was unlawful, more than 90 (later about 140) people, some with serious convictions, were released. The government rushed through curfew and ankle-monitor laws and later a preventative detention regime. On 22 November O'Neil said she had considered releasing the NZYQ plaintiff to avoid a broader ruling ('It was considered and we decided not to do it') and clarified that earlier remarks about acting on 'legal advice' had been misleading, as she had been referring to 'operational and policy conversations'. Shadow attorney-general Michaelia Cash said the government had 'botched' its response.
items.response: O'Neil and Giles said the government was 'moving quickly to finalise a tough preventative detention regime' and announced a $255 million response package.
items.outcome: Legislation passed in November–December 2023; no formal finding against either minister. Both were moved from the portfolios in July 2024.

items.portfolio: Minister for Industry and Science
items.title: Husic says Palestinians are being 'collectively punished', prompting Opposition criticism
items.summary: On 19 October 2023 Husic said he felt 'very strongly that Palestinians are being collectively punished here for Hamas' barbarism' and that Australia should 'speak up for Palestinians', while condemning Hamas and supporting Israel's right to defend itself. Opposition deputy leader Sussan Ley accused him of 'freelancing on foreign policy' and Peter Dutton said the comments showed 'deep division' in Labor; the Executive Council of Australian Jewry described his statements as 'very troublesome for the community'.
items.response: Husic stood by the remarks. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said 'every innocent life matters'; Home Affairs Minister Clare O'Neil declined to endorse the 'collective punishment' characterisation.
items.outcome: No formal finding. Husic was dropped from cabinet after the May 2025 election in a factional decision he later said was partly linked to his views on Gaza.

items.portfolio: Minister for Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development and Local Government
items.title: King's rejection of extra Qatar Airways flights scrutinised amid Qantas lobbying claims
items.summary: In July 2023 King rejected Qatar Airways' request for 28 additional weekly flights to Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, citing the national interest. Amid high airfares and evidence that Qantas had lobbied against the bid, a Senate select committee examined the decision; Virgin Australia's CEO testified King had relayed that Alan Joyce was 'not happy'. King declined to appear, saying it is 'long-standing practice that House of Representatives members do not appear before Senate committees'. The committee's 9 October 2023 report found 'the national interest would have been well served by agreeing to Qatar's request' and recommended an immediate review.
items.response: King called the inquiry 'a political stunt from the Coalition' and a 'ridiculous farce', saying she was 'doing the hard work'; Labor senators issued a dissenting report citing 'inaccuracies and obvious bias'.
items.outcome: Senate committee recommendations; government did not reverse the decision. No formal finding of misconduct.

items.portfolio: Prime Minister
items.title: PM's adult son granted Qantas Chairman's Lounge membership
items.summary: In August–September 2023 it was reported that Qantas had granted Chairman's Lounge membership to the Prime Minister's adult son, Nathan, a decision requiring sign-off by senior Qantas leadership; parliamentarians and their spouses are routinely invited but other family members are not. The revelation came during a Senate inquiry into Qantas, at which five of seven committee senators had declared their own membership. Joe Aston's October 2024 book later alleged Albanese had asked Alan Joyce for the membership in 2022.
items.response: Albanese did not deny the 2024 claim that he asked for the membership; his spokesperson dismissed Opposition calls for a referral as 'a pathetic attempt at creating a headline'.
items.outcome: No formal finding; membership was disclosed.

items.portfolio: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence
items.title: Marles' $3.6m in RAAF VIP flights, including trips to Avalon near his Geelong home
items.summary: Documents obtained by Greens senator David Shoebridge showed Marles' office had spent more than $3 million on RAAF special purpose flights since April 2022, second only to the Prime Minister. Capital Brief later reported via FOI that 155 flights cost $3.6 million between April 2022 and June 2023, with flight-tracker data showing more than 70 movements to or from Avalon Airport near Geelong; Defence declined to release routes citing an AFP security review. Shadow defence minister Andrew Hastie also questioned whether Marles carried golf clubs on VIP flights after photos of him golfing in Cambodia.
items.response: Marles said 'a lot of people travel on those flights, my direct component is a fraction of the number that has been reported' and 'everywhere I have gone, everything I have done has been on behalf of the Australian people', noting comparable spending by predecessors Peter Dutton and Barnaby Joyce.
items.outcome: No formal finding; flights were within entitlements.

items.portfolio: Minister for Finance, Minister for Women, Minister for the Public Service
items.title: Gallagher accused of misleading Senate over prior knowledge of Higgins allegation
items.summary: Private messages between Brittany Higgins and her partner David Sharaz, leaked to The Australian in June 2023, indicated the pair contacted Gallagher days before Higgins' allegation became public in February 2021. At Senate estimates on 4 June 2021 Gallagher had told Senator Linda Reynolds 'no one had any knowledge. How dare you?'. The Coalition accused her of misleading Parliament and of collusion.
items.response: In a Senate statement on 13 June 2023 Gallagher said she had received a 'heads up' but 'I did nothing with that information. Absolutely nothing,' and 'I did not mislead the Senate at Senate estimates on June the 4th, 2021.'
items.outcome: No referral to the Privileges Committee proceeded; no formal finding.

items.portfolio: Minister for Communications
items.title: Rowland accepted Sportsbet dinner and $10,000 donation before 2022 election
items.summary: Nine newspapers reported on 9 February 2023 that Sportsbet paid about $8,960 for a dinner supporting Rowland's campaign in March 2022 and donated $10,000 in the days before the May 2022 election, both below the $15,000 disclosure threshold. As Communications Minister Rowland is responsible for online gambling regulation. Independent MP Andrew Wilkie said her position was 'patently untenable' and Greens senator Larissa Waters said it was 'clearly untenable for the minister to remain as gambling regulator'.
items.response: Rowland's spokesperson said all donations were 'compliant with the disclosure requirements of the AEC' and that she was not in breach of the ministerial code. On 20 February 2023 Rowland said: 'I will not take money from Sportsbet' in future.
items.outcome: No formal finding; Rowland retained the portfolio and later became Attorney-General.

items.portfolio: Attorney-General
items.title: Dreyfus' approval of $2.4m Higgins settlement referred to NACC; no corruption issue found
items.summary: In December 2022 the Commonwealth settled Brittany Higgins' compensation claim for $2.4 million after a one-day mediation from which former minister Linda Reynolds was excluded. Peter Dutton and others questioned the speed and size of the payout, and Reynolds referred Dreyfus' handling of the process to the National Anti-Corruption Commission. Reynolds' Federal Court claim against the Commonwealth in 2025 alleged Dreyfus had a conflict of interest and committed misfeasance; those allegations were removed from the claim in November 2025.
items.response: The NACC said 'The then-attorney-general approved the settlement in accordance with the departmental advice' and there was no inappropriate ministerial intervention. Dreyfus (by then out of the ministry) criticised the NACC over the time taken.
items.outcome: NACC found on 12 June 2025 that 'no corruption issue arises'. Allegations against Dreyfus were dropped from Reynolds' lawsuit in November 2025.

items.portfolio: Incoming Minister for the Environment and Water (Labor frontbencher; sworn in 1 June 2022)
items.title: Plibersek apologises for saying Peter Dutton 'looks a bit like Voldemort'
items.summary: Days after the May 2022 election, Plibersek told Nine Radio (4BC) that with Dutton set to become Opposition Leader, 'there will be a lot of children who have watched a lot of Harry Potter films who will be very frightened of what they are seeing on TV at night' and 'he looks a bit like Voldemort'. She was a Labor frontbencher at the time and was sworn in as a minister on 1 June 2022.
items.response: Plibersek phoned Dutton to apologise and told 2GB 'I shouldn't have said it'. Albanese said the comment was unacceptable and that she did the right thing by apologising, saying he wanted to 'change the way that politics functions in this country'.
items.outcome: Private and public apology; Dutton said it was 'water off a duck's back'.
